passage:
Trisha,
I'm writing this instead of texting, because texting is kind of the problem. On Friday, when you didn't answer for two hours, I checked my phone maybe forty times. I made up a whole story: you were bored of me, you liked someone from your art class. So I posted that photo with Kunal's arm round my shoulder, hoping you'd see it and feel what I felt. That was a test, and it wasn't fair. You were at your nani's with no signal. I'm trying something the school counsellor suggested: when the dread starts, I put the phone in a drawer, walk round the block and ask what I actually know. I really like you. I don't want to smother this.
Sarika

qa.q: Where was Trisha on Friday?
qa.a: At her nani's, with no signal.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling during the two hours without a reply?
qa.a: Sarika felt dread and jealousy, imagining Trisha was bored or liked someone else, and checked the phone about forty times.

qa.q: What small step is Sarika trying for next time?
qa.a: Putting the phone in a drawer, walking round the block and asking what is actually known before reacting.

qa.q: How might Trisha have felt seeing the photo with Kunal?
qa.a: Trisha was probably confused and hurt, having done nothing wrong except being somewhere with no signal.

grounding: Shows a teen who checks messages constantly, dreads a delayed reply and tests a partner with jealousy, then learns to self-soothe.

passage: Okay, don't laugh. You know how Dhruv takes forever to reply? Last week he saw my message at 8:14 and said nothing until ten. I'm Neelam, I'm fifteen, and I spent those two hours refreshing the screen like a crazy person, sure he'd found someone better. Then I did something dumb. I told him Aman from tuition had offered to walk me home, just to see if he'd care. He did care. He got upset, and I felt awful, because all I really wanted was for him to say he missed me. So now I've got a rule. When my stomach does that drop, I put on music and sketch for twenty minutes before I touch the phone. Mostly he's replied by then. And if he hasn't, I'm calmer anyway.

qa.q: When did Dhruv see Neelam's message?
What was Neelam really wanting when the story about Aman came out?
qa.a: Neelam wanted closeness and reassurance, hoping Dhruv would say he missed Neelam, but the test only led to feeling awful.

qa.q: How does Neelam's new rule help?
qa.a: Sketching to music for twenty minutes gives the panic time to settle, so Neelam doesn't act on the fear.

qa.q: How might Dhruv have felt hearing about Aman?
qa.a: Dhruv likely felt jealous and upset, not knowing it was a test.

grounding: Illustrates a teen who dreads delayed replies, tests with jealousy and then learns a way to self-soothe.

passage:
Monday: Yusuf's reply took three hours, and Sarika spent them flipping her phone face-up, face-down on the desk, homework untouched. When he finally wrote, "sorry, cricket practice," she typed back "k" and posted a picture of herself laughing with his friend Omar, to see if he'd notice.
Thursday: The dread came again during a free period. This time Sarika wrote the feeling in the back of her notebook, "scared he's losing interest", and went to the canteen with her cousin.
The next Sunday: She told Yusuf plainly, "When you go quiet I panic a bit. Can you just say if you're busy?" He sent "busy, talk at 7" that evening, and called at seven. She went back to her book.

qa.q: What did Sarika write in the back of her notebook?
qa.a: "scared he's losing interest"

qa.q: Why did Sarika post the picture with Omar on Monday?
qa.a: She was anxious and jealous after the long silence and wanted to test whether Yusuf would notice and care.

qa.q: Which change helped Sarika most, and why?
qa.a: Naming the fear on paper and then asking Yusuf directly, because it calmed the panic and got her a simple answer.

qa.q: How might Yusuf see Sarika's Sunday message?
qa.a: He probably finds it easy to agree, because a clear request is simpler than guessing why she sent "k".

grounding: Shows over several days a teen moving from anxious checking and jealousy tests to self-soothing and asking directly.

passage:
Dear Harsha,
You asked how things are with Vikram, so here's the honest version. Last Tuesday he didn't reply all evening. I had three texts sent and a fourth typed: "Fine, forget it." My thumb was on send. Then I did the thing we used to laugh about in Class 9: I wrote down what I was actually scared of. "That I'm not important to him." Seeing it on paper made it smaller. I deleted the fourth text. Next day I told him, "When you vanish, I get scared. Can you tell me if you're busy?" He said yes, easily. Also, I've rejoined the basketball team, and my Saturdays are mine again. Write back soon.
Ankita

qa.q: What did the fourth text say?
qa.a: "Fine, forget it."

qa.q: What was Ankita afraid of under the urge to send the fourth text?
qa.a: Ankita was scared of not being important to Vikram, and writing it down made the fear feel smaller.

qa.q: Which steps did Ankita take that worked?
qa.a: Pausing, naming the fear on paper, deleting the angry text and asking Vikram directly to say when busy.

qa.q: How might Vikram feel getting a clear request instead of an angry fourth text?
qa.a: He probably feels relieved and more willing to help, since he could agree easily instead of defending himself.

grounding: Shows a teen pausing before a fourth text, naming the fear, asking directly and building a life beyond one relationship.

passage: People think this only happens with girlfriends. For me it was my best friend, Keerthana. I'm Wasim, Class 11, and last year if she didn't answer by lunch I'd assume she'd dropped me for the debate crowd. Message after message. One day I had three unanswered and was typing a fourth, something sarcastic, when my sister said, "Put it down. What are you actually scared of?" I said, "That she doesn't need me." Saying it out loud felt silly, and also lighter. So I asked Keerthana straight: "Are we okay? I get jumpy when you go quiet." She laughed and said her phone had been taken in class. Since then I've joined the photography club. It helps to have more than one person in my world.

qa.q: What was Wasim typing when the sister spoke?
qa.a: A fourth message, something sarcastic.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel after saying the fear out loud?
qa.a: Wasim felt silly but also lighter, because naming the fear took away some of its power.

qa.q: What would you advise someone in Wasim's place, based on what worked?
qa.a: Pause before the next message, name the fear and ask the friend directly, while also building other friendships and interests.

qa.q: How does Keerthana seem to react to Wasim's direct question?
qa.a: Keerthana takes it lightly and laughs, explaining her phone was taken, which suggests the friendship was never in danger.

grounding: Illustrates a teen calming the alarm by pausing, naming the fear, asking directly and widening life beyond one friend.

passage: I'm Pankaj, and I share a wall with my cousin Amandeep, so I hear things. Last month, every evening, it was the ping-ping-ping of her messages to her boyfriend, then silence, then her pacing. Last Friday was different. Through the open door I saw her, phone in hand, thumb hovering. Then she put it face-down, picked up her guitar and played the same four chords for about ten minutes. Later I heard her on a call, quiet and clear: "When you don't reply, I start thinking the worst. Can we agree you'll say if you're busy?" I can't know exactly what she felt. But she came out for dinner smiling and asked me to come to her Sunday jam with her school friends.

qa.q: What did Amandeep pick up after putting the phone face-down?
qa.a: Her guitar.

qa.q: What might Amandeep have been feeling while her thumb hovered over the phone?
qa.a: She was probably anxious about the silence, but chose to calm herself before sending anything.

qa.q: What did Amandeep do that a teen in a similar spot could copy?
qa.a: Pause, soothe the panic with something absorbing, then ask the other person clearly for what is needed.

qa.q: How does Pankaj see the change in Amandeep?
qa.a: Pankaj notices the pacing replaced by calm, a clear call and a new interest in sharing her music with friends, without being sure what she felt.

grounding: Shows through an observer a teen pausing before texting, asking directly and turning to interests and friends.

subtype: Fear of abandonment in adult love [Actor]
passage: Sit, beta, since you asked why your Dada and I still hold hands. At twenty I was a nightmare to love. If Chetan came to the college gate five minutes late, I decided he was bored of me. If he laughed with a classmate, I went silent for two days, then burst out with cruel things, then cried in the hostel bathroom, ashamed. Once I threw his letters back at him in the library. He didn't shout. He picked them up and said, "Damini, I'm not going anywhere. But you must tell me when you're scared, not punish me." That was my turning point. I began saying, "I'm frightened you'll leave," out loud. It sounded foolish. It worked, slowly, over years.

qa.q: What did young Damini throw back at Chetan in the library?
qa.a: His letters.

qa.q: What did young Damini feel after the silences and cruel words?
qa.a: She felt ashamed, crying in the hostel bathroom, because under the anger was fear of being left.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Chetan asked Damini to say when she was scared instead of punishing him, and she began naming the fear out loud.

qa.q: How might Chetan have felt picking up the letters?
qa.a: He was likely hurt but steady, choosing to reassure her and set a clear request rather than walk away.

grounding: Shows a young adult who reads small cues as rejection, lashes out, feels shame, and softens with a safe partner and self-awareness.

subtype: Fear of abandonment in adult love [Actor]
passage: Irfan's train to Kolkata ran through the night, twenty hours, most of it without network. He had warned her. Still, when his good-night message didn't come, Reena lay awake rereading his last text, "ok ttyl". He usually wrote more. By two in the morning she had sent six messages, the last one: "Fine, just say you're done with me." In the morning they all showed as read at once, and his reply came: "Reena?? No signal for hours. What happened?" Her face burned. She typed and deleted three excuses. Then she wrote the truth: "I got scared you were leaving. I'm sorry about that last message. I'm working on it." He called from the next station.

qa.q: How many messages had Reena sent by two in the morning?
qa.a: Six messages.

qa.q: How did Reena feel when Irfan's reply came?
qa.a: She felt ashamed, her face burning, after reading a short text and silence as rejection.

qa.q: Which choice helped repair things, and why?
qa.a: Writing the truth about being scared instead of an excuse, because it let Irfan understand and respond warmly.

qa.q: What is it like for Irfan to wake up to six messages?
qa.a: He is probably confused and worried, since he had warned her about the network and did nothing wrong.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who reads a short text and silence as rejection, lashes out and feels shame, then names the fear.

subtype: Fear of abandonment in adult love [Actor]
passage: At Zubin's cousin's engagement in Bandra, he spent ten minutes on the balcony talking to an old college friend, and Zeenat felt the whole evening tilt. She stood by the snacks, smiling stiffly, counting. When he came back she said, too loudly, "Go on, she's more interesting." Two aunties turned. In the taxi she stared out at the dark sea, cheeks hot, wanting to disappear. Zubin was quiet a while, then said, "That hurt. But I think you got scared." She nodded, eyes stinging. "You talk to anyone for ten minutes and my brain says you're leaving." He took her hand. That week she began writing down each time it happened, and what had actually been true.

qa.q: How long did Zubin talk to the old college friend?
qa.a: Ten minutes.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling in the taxi?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and embarrassed, cheeks hot, knowing her fear of being left had made her lash out.

qa.q: What small step did Zeenat take afterwards?
qa.a: She started writing down each time the fear came and what had actually been true, to build self-awareness.

qa.q: How does Zubin respond to Zeenat's outburst?
qa.a: He admits it hurt but sees the fear under it and takes her hand, which makes it safer for her to be honest.

grounding: Shows a young adult reading a small cue as rejection, lashing out, feeling shame, then softening with self-awareness and a safe partner.

passage: Urmila's phone buzzed right through the team lunch in Gurugram: "Where are you?" "Who's there?" "Send a pic?" Each time she replied, and each time she felt more like a suspect. By dessert she had switched the phone to silent. At home, her partner Swati was waiting on the sofa, eyes red. "You went quiet. I thought..." Urmila felt the old urge to walk straight to the bedroom and shut the door. Instead she sat down beside her. "I love you. I'm not going anywhere. And I can't send photos from every lunch; it makes me feel watched." She paused. "I'll text once when I get there and once when I leave. That's a promise I can keep." Swati's shoulders loosened, a little.

qa.q: What did Urmila do with her phone by dessert?
qa.a: She switched the phone to silent.

qa.q: How did Urmila feel as the messages kept coming?
qa.a: She felt watched and like a suspect, and was tempted to withdraw by shutting the bedroom door.

qa.q: Why did Urmila's approach at home work better than withdrawing?
qa.a: She stayed close and warm while setting a clear, keepable limit, which reassured Swati without giving in to every demand.

qa.q: What is it like for Swati when Urmila goes quiet at lunch?
qa.a: Swati seems frightened and tearful, reading the silence as a sign of being left.

grounding: Shows a partner who feels watched by an anxious partner and chooses warm consistency with clear limits instead of withdrawing.

passage:
"Nazia, your phone's lit up four times since the samosas came."
"It's Faisal. He wants to know when I'll be home."
"It's six-thirty."
"I know." Nazia turned the phone over. "Every evening it's like an exam. Did I reply fast enough, did I say 'love you' back. Some days I want to hide in the office till nine."
Her elder sister Alka poured more chai. "And if you did hide?"
"He'd panic more. Then I'd feel worse. I do love him, Alka."
"So tell him that. And tell him the limit. Not in the middle of a fight."
"Like, 'I'll call when I leave work, but I won't answer ten texts in a meeting'?"
"Exactly that. Warm, and clear."
Nazia typed slowly, then looked up. "He sent back a heart. Just one."

qa.q: How many times had Nazia's phone lit up since the samosas came?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: What does Nazia's wish to hide in the office till nine suggest she feels?
qa.a: She feels pressured and tested, as if every evening were an exam of her love.

qa.q: What advice did Alka give, and why might it help?
qa.a: Tell Faisal the love and the limit calmly, not in a fight, so he gets reassurance and a clear boundary.

qa.q: Why might Faisal react better to the calm message than to Nazia hiding?
qa.a: A warm, clear message reassures him, while hiding would feed his fear of being left and make him check more.

grounding: Illustrates a partner who feels watched and pushed to prove love, and learns warm consistency with a clear limit.

passage: The worst month was March. Suraj would ask, three times a night, "You still love me, right?" and I'd say yes, and it never seemed to land. I started staying late at the office, telling myself I needed the quiet. I'm Deepak, and I'm not proud of that. The later I came home, the more Suraj checked where I was, and the more trapped I felt. One night he said, "You're leaving, I can tell," and I saw that my hiding had built the very thing he feared. So we changed it. I come home by eight and say so warmly. I also said, "I won't answer the same question every hour. Ask me once, and trust the answer." It's slower than I hoped. But it's better.

qa.q: By what time does Deepak now come home?
qa.a: By eight.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel as Suraj checked more and more?
qa.a: Deepak felt trapped and pressured, and stayed late at the office to escape.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and what helped fix it?
qa.a: Pulling away confirmed Suraj's fear; coming home at a steady time warmly while setting a limit on repeated questions helped.

qa.q: How does Deepak's staying late affect Suraj?
qa.a: It makes Suraj more frightened of being left, so he checks more and finally says, "You're leaving, I can tell."

grounding: Shows a partner who withdraws under pressure, sees it confirm the other's fear, and shifts to warm consistency with clear limits.

subtype: Toddler who does not seek comfort [Actor]
passage: When his mother, Indu, left for the office, Sumit didn't cry. He sat on the mat of the Andheri flat stacking cups and did not look up. Later he slipped on the balcony step and grazed his knee. His lip trembled, but he turned away from the nanny's open arms and crawled behind the sofa. When Indu came home, he glanced at her once, then went on lining up his cars, cheeks still blotchy.

qa.q: Where did Sumit crawl after grazing his knee?
qa.a: Behind the sofa.

qa.q: What do Sumit's trembling lip and blotchy cheeks suggest?
qa.a: That he was hurt and upset inside, even though he looked calm and did not seek comfort.

qa.q: How could Indu gently help Sumit over time?
qa.a: Stay close and offer comfort calmly and often, without forcing it, so he learns that showing need brings care.

qa.q: What is it like for the nanny when Sumit turns away from her arms?
qa.a: The nanny may feel rejected or worried, unsure how to comfort a child who hides his hurt.

grounding: Shows a toddler who seems unbothered at parting and turns away from comfort when hurt, while small cues show stress.

subtype: Toddler who does not seek comfort [Actor]
passage:
"He didn't even look up when you left, Ritu," Dadi said.
"He never does." Ritu watched Santosh push a toy bus across the tiles. "Santosh, Mummy's home!"
He kept pushing the bus.
"He bumped his head on the table at eleven," Dadi said. "No crying. He sat in the corner with his blanket."
"Alone?"
"Cheeks red. Holding the blanket very tight."
Ritu knelt near him. "That hurt, na?" Santosh stiffened and turned his back. She stayed close, not touching.

qa.q: What did Santosh do after bumping his head?
qa.a: He sat in the corner with his blanket.

qa.q: What does Santosh holding the blanket very tight suggest?
qa.a: That he was hurt and stressed, even though he didn't cry or come to anyone.

qa.q: What did Ritu do that could help over time?
qa.a: She named the hurt and stayed close without forcing a touch, letting Santosh come when ready.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel watching Santosh sit alone after the bump?
qa.a: Dadi seems worried, noticing his red cheeks and tight grip even though he didn't cry.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler who does not seek comfort when hurt and seems unbothered at parting, with stress visible in small cues.

subtype: Toddler who does not seek comfort [Actor]
passage: Crèche note, Friday. Deepika's father, Saurabh, left at nine; she did not watch him go. She played with the dough alone all morning. At eleven another child pushed her and she fell hard. She did not cry or come to me. She sat very still, jaw tight, pressing her own palm, and turned her face when I reached out. I sat down near her with the dough and waited. After a while she leaned slightly against my arm. I told Saurabh at pickup, and we agreed to keep offering comfort gently.

qa.q: What did Deepika play with all morning?
qa.a: The dough.

qa.q: What do Deepika's tight jaw and pressed palm suggest she was feeling after the fall?
qa.a: She was likely hurt and stressed, even though she did not cry or ask for comfort.

qa.q: Which choice of the note-writer's worked, and why?
qa.a: Sitting nearby and waiting instead of pushing a hug, because it let Deepika lean in when she was ready.

qa.q: What is it like for Saurabh to hear about the fall at pickup?
qa.a: Saurabh may be surprised and concerned, since Deepika shows so little need that her hurt is easy to miss.

grounding: Shows a toddler who plays alone at parting and turns from comfort when hurt, with a caregiver offering gentle closeness.

passage: Wanjiru would not let anyone zip her jacket at the Nairobi kindergarten. "I do it," she said, struggling for five minutes while the others ran out to play. When her mother's promised visit on Sports Day didn't happen, Wanjiru wiped her eyes fast with her sleeve and turned to the wall. Ms Freya knelt and opened her arms. Wanjiru stepped back. "I'm not sad. I can do the sack race by myself." She did, alone, and didn't look at the empty chair by the fence.

qa.q: What did Wanjiru say when Ms Freya opened her arms?
qa.a: "I'm not sad. I can do the sack race by myself."

qa.q: What was Wanjiru feeling when she wiped her eyes and turned to the wall?
qa.a: She was disappointed and hurt that her mother didn't come, but hid it to seem strong.

qa.q: How could Ms Freya support Wanjiru without pushing?
qa.a: Stay nearby, cheer her race and let her know comfort is there whenever she wants it.

qa.q: How might Ms Freya feel when Wanjiru steps back from the hug?
qa.a: Ms Freya may feel concerned, sensing that Wanjiru's independence is guarding against more disappointment.

grounding: Shows a young child who insists on doing things alone, hides tears and pulls away from a hug after a disappointment.

passage: In the clinic waiting room, Rajni pulled her hand out of her mother's. "I can sit alone." When the nurse called her name, she marched in first, chin up. The injection pricked; her eyes filled, but she pressed her lips together and stared at the chart of animals on the wall. Damini reached out to hug her. Rajni twisted away and climbed down from the bed herself. Only in the auto home, when she thought no one was looking, did a tear slide down, and she rubbed it off quickly.

qa.q: What did Rajni stare at after the injection?
qa.a: The chart of animals on the wall.

qa.q: Why might Rajni rub the tear off so quickly?
qa.a: She seems to want to look strong and hide that she was hurt and scared, perhaps guarding against disappointment.

qa.q: How could Damini respond when Rajni twists away?
qa.a: Stay close and calm, say it's okay to cry, and leave the hug on offer without insisting.

qa.q: What is it like for Damini when Rajni pulls away from her hug?
qa.a: Damini may feel hurt or pushed away, even though Rajni is the one hiding her pain.

grounding: Illustrates a child who insists on doing things alone, hides tears and pulls away from a parent's hug when upset.

passage:
Monday: Shankar fell off the swing at the colony park and scraped both palms. When his grandmother, Rukmini, hurried over, he shoved her hand away. "I'm fine." He walked home holding his hands behind his back.
Thursday: He spent fifteen minutes trying to tie his own laces and wouldn't let her help, face red. When the school van left without him, he said, "I don't care," and went quiet.
The next Sunday: Rukmini didn't reach for him. She just sat on the step with a bowl of peanuts. After a long while Shankar sat beside her, close enough that their elbows touched.

qa.q: What did Rukmini sit with on Sunday?
qa.a: A bowl of peanuts.

qa.q: What might Shankar be feeling when he says "I don't care" about the van?
qa.a: He is probably upset and disappointed, but hides it to seem like he doesn't need anyone.

qa.q: Which choice of Rukmini's worked, and why?
qa.a: Sitting nearby without reaching for him, because it let Shankar come close on his own terms.

qa.q: What is it like for Rukmini when Shankar shoves her hand away?
qa.a: She may feel hurt and worried, wanting to help a child who won't let her.

grounding: Shows over several days a young child who hides hurt and refuses help, and slowly comes closer when not pressed.

passage: Everyone in Year 5 in Leeds had got an invitation to Felix's birthday except Emeka. "Don't care," he told his dad at the school gate, hitching his bag higher. "Parties are boring." At home he went straight to the tablet and played the racing game for two hours, jaw tight, jabbing at the screen. His father didn't take the tablet away or push. He brought two bowls of jollof rice, sat on the arm of the sofa and said, "If you ever feel like talking about Felix's party, I'm around. No rush." Emeka kept racing. But at bedtime he said, very quietly, "It was only me who didn't get one."

qa.q: How long did Emeka play the racing game?
qa.a: For two hours.

qa.q: What does Emeka's tight jaw while playing suggest?
qa.a: That he was hurt and left out, even though he said he didn't care.

qa.q: Which choice of his father's worked, and why?
qa.a: Offering to talk with no pressure, because it let Emeka share the hurt at bedtime in his own time.

qa.q: How might Emeka's father feel hearing the quiet sentence at bedtime?
qa.a: He may feel sad for Emeka and also glad the invitation to talk was finally taken up.

grounding: Shows a child who claims not to care about being left out and buries it in a game, while an adult invites feelings without pressure.

passage: At the district swimming club, the relay list went up on the board, and Charu's name wasn't on it. The other girls crowded round, squealing. Charu shrugged. "Relays are stupid anyway." She sat on the changing-room bench, earphones in, playing a puzzle game on her phone with fierce attention. Coach Ganga saw that she didn't look up for twenty minutes. She didn't lecture. She sat at the other end of the bench, sorting kickboards. "I'm here till six," she said. "If you want to talk about the list, or not, either's fine." Charu kept tapping. On her way out, she stopped. "Can I train with the relay girls anyway?"

qa.q: What was Charu playing on her phone?
qa.a: A puzzle game.

qa.q: What might Charu be feeling behind "Relays are stupid anyway"?
qa.a: She is probably disappointed and hurt at being left off the list, hiding it behind the game.

qa.q: How did Coach Ganga invite Charu's feelings without pressure?
qa.a: By sitting nearby, busy with kickboards, and saying she was available to talk or not until six.

qa.q: How might the other girls see Charu's shrug?
qa.a: They might think she really doesn't care, missing that she was hurt.

grounding: Illustrates a child brushing off being left out by burying it in a phone game, while an adult stays available without pushing.

passage:
Saturday: The colony boys picked teams and left Ojas out. "Whatever. I'd rather play on the computer," he said, and spent the afternoon building a fortress in his game, door shut. His elder brother Dhruv knocked once. "Snacks, if you want." No answer.
The next Wednesday: While they brushed their teeth, Dhruv mentioned, "I got dropped from the team in Class 5. It stung for ages." Ojas said nothing, but didn't leave.
The Sunday after: Ojas came and sat on Dhruv's bed. "They said I'm too slow," he muttered. Dhruv listened and didn't try to fix it. Later they went down together to bowl at the wall.

qa.q: What did Ojas build in his game on Saturday?
qa.a: A fortress.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling behind "Whatever"?
qa.a: He was hurt and ashamed about being left out, hiding it in the game behind a shut door.

qa.q: What did Dhruv do that helped Ojas open up?
qa.a: He offered snacks without pushing, shared his own story of being dropped and later just listened.

qa.q: How might Dhruv feel when Ojas finally sits on his bed?
qa.a: Dhruv may feel relieved and trusted, since his patient invitations worked.

grounding: Shows over days a child who hides being left out in a game and slowly opens up when invited without pressure.

passage: In Ms Elif's third-grade class in Izmir, Ada never raised her hand for help. When her tower of blocks for the science project collapsed, she rebuilt it, face blank. When a classmate tore her drawing, she said, "It's fine," and started again. Elif noticed the pencil pressed hard enough to rip the new paper. She didn't ask "What's wrong?" in front of everyone. At the end of the day she left a note on Ada's desk: "I'm in the classroom at lunch on Tuesdays and Thursdays if you want to draw with me. Your choice." The first Tuesday the room stayed empty. On Thursday, Ada came in, sat two desks away and drew in silence.

qa.q: On which days did Ms Elif offer lunchtime drawing?
qa.a: Tuesdays and Thursdays.

qa.q: What was Elif thinking when she saw the pencil ripping the paper?
qa.a: She was concerned, sensing that Ada was upset under her blank face and "It's fine".

qa.q: Which choice of Elif's worked, and why?
qa.a: A private note with a choice and steady times, because it gave Ada a safe way to come closer without pressure.

qa.q: What might it be like for Ada to walk in on Thursday?
qa.a: Ada probably felt cautious but curious, testing whether the offer was real by sitting two desks away.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a self-contained child and using a quiet, steady offer with a choice so the child can come closer.

passage: At the hostel school in Darjeeling, Tenzin-sir had taught Zeenat maths for two terms and never once seen her ask for help. When her mother's call was cancelled on visiting Sunday, she said, "Okay," and went to do her laundry. When she got a fraction sum wrong on the board, she erased it and stood still, face calm, till he moved on. So he stopped asking "Any doubts?" to the whole class. Instead, during practice, he stopped by her desk: "Want a hint, or want to try once more first?" She usually chose to try. By the second month she began leaving a small question mark in her notebook margin, where only he would see it.

qa.q: What did Zeenat do after her mother's call was cancelled?
qa.a: She said, "Okay," and went to do her laundry.

qa.q: What was Tenzin-sir thinking when Zeenat stood still after the wrong sum?
qa.a: He was concerned that she never asked for help and seemed fine even when upset, so he changed how he offered help.

qa.q: Why does offering a choice work better than asking the whole class for doubts?
qa.a: It lets Zeenat accept help privately and on her own terms, without being exposed.

qa.q: What does the small question mark show about how Zeenat feels?
qa.a: That she is beginning to trust Tenzin-sir enough to ask for help, in a way that feels safe to her.

grounding: Illustrates a teacher who notices a child who never asks for help and uses quiet check-ins and choices.

passage: I'm Ganga, the trainee teacher in Class 6-C this term, so mostly I watch. Nazia is the girl everyone calls "no trouble". She finishes her work, never asks anything, and when her group's poster got ripped on Monday she said, "It's okay," before anyone else spoke. But I noticed she didn't eat her lunch that day, and she picked at the edge of her sleeve all afternoon. I can't know what she felt. I tried not to crowd her. I asked, "Do you want to redo the poster at your desk or at the back table?" She chose the back table, which is near mine. The next day she sat there again without being asked, and once, very quietly, asked me how to spell "volcano".

qa.q: Where did Nazia choose to redo the poster?
qa.a: At the back table.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling on noticing the uneaten lunch and picked sleeve?
qa.a: Ganga felt concerned, sensing Nazia might be upset despite saying "It's okay", but was careful not to assume.

qa.q: What made Ganga's approach work?
qa.a: Offering a simple choice instead of a demand and being steadily nearby, which let Nazia come closer.

qa.q: How might Nazia see the back table the next day?
qa.a: Nazia seems to find it a safe spot near a steady adult, where asking a small question feels possible.

grounding: Shows an observer noticing a child who looks fine during upsets and offering choices and steady availability.

passage: Coach's note, Thursday. Pooja is my most reliable player, and she handles everything alone. This week her doubles partner, Nirmala, cried in the changing room about trouble at home and hugged Pooja. Since then Pooja has come early and left early, practising serves by herself. When Nirmala waved, Pooja studied her racquet strings. I asked Pooja to stay back. She said, "I'm just not a hugging person. I don't want to be anyone's crutch." I didn't argue. I suggested one small thing: tell Nirmala one true sentence, like "I don't know what to say, but I'm here." Today I saw her say something to Nirmala at the net. It was short. Nirmala smiled.

qa.q: What did Pooja study when Nirmala waved?
qa.a: Her racquet strings.

qa.q: What does Pooja's "I don't want to be anyone's crutch" suggest she feels?
qa.a: She seems uneasy and a little trapped by closeness, worried that being leaned on will cost her freedom.

qa.q: What small step did the coach suggest, and why might it help?
qa.a: Saying one true sentence to Nirmala, because it lets Pooja practise closeness without feeling overwhelmed.

qa.q: What is it like for Nirmala when Pooja avoids her after the hug?
qa.a: Nirmala may feel rejected and confused, having just shared something painful.

grounding: Shows a teen who pulls back after a friend gets emotional and practises vulnerability in a small step.

passage:
Wednesday night. Pradeep asked again today why I've been skipping lunch with the group. I said "Busy" and put my earphones in. The truth: I failed the chem unit test, and I'd rather sort it alone than have everyone being nice at me. When people get all soft and concerned, I feel like the walls are closing in. But Pradeep looked properly hurt, and said, "You know everything about my stuff. I know nothing about yours." That stuck. So, small step: tomorrow I'll tell him about the test. Just the test. Not the rest of it. Not yet.
Manoj

qa.q: What test did Manoj fail?
qa.a: The chem unit test.

qa.q: How does Manoj feel when people get soft and concerned?
qa.a: Manoj feels trapped, as if the walls are closing in, and prefers to handle problems alone.

qa.q: Why is telling Pradeep only about the test a good first step?
qa.a: It is small enough to feel safe, so Manoj can practise opening up without feeling overwhelmed.

qa.q: What is it like for Pradeep when Manoj says "Busy"?
qa.a: Pradeep feels hurt and shut out, since he shares everything and gets nothing back.

grounding: Illustrates a teen who withdraws when a friendship gets close and plans a small step towards vulnerability.

passage: When Mehak asked if I'd come to her sister's wedding in Jaipur and meet everyone, I heard myself say, "Let's not get heavy." Two weeks later I ended it, by text, from the library. I told my roommate I needed my freedom, that I'd never been one for all that. I'm Sabina, twenty-one, and here's what I didn't say: that night I ate dinner alone in the hostel mess and felt like the loneliest person in the building. I think I left because being needed felt like a trap, and needing her felt worse, like standing at the edge of something with no railing. I'm not ready to fix it. I'm starting to see it, at least.

qa.q: Where was Mehak's sister's wedding?
qa.a: In Jaipur.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling underneath the talk of freedom?
qa.a: Sabina felt deeply lonely and afraid of depending on Mehak, not a lack of feeling.

qa.q: What could Sabina try next, now that the pattern is clearer?
qa.a: Talk it through with a trusted friend or counsellor, and practise saying small true things before walking away.

qa.q: How might Mehak have experienced a break-up by text after the wedding invitation?
qa.a: Mehak probably felt shocked and hurt, having asked for more closeness and been left instead.

grounding: Shows a young adult who avoids deep talk and leaves when a partner asks for more, while feeling lonely and afraid of dependence.

passage:
Warden's note, Room 214. Disha, second year, is fiercely independent: fixes her own fan, never asks for anything, eats early to avoid the crowd. Tonight her boyfriend waited at the gate for an hour. The guard said he wanted to "talk about where this is going". Disha sent word she was busy, then sat in the common room with a book she never turned a page of. When I asked if she was all right, she said, "I just don't do the needy stuff." Later I heard her on the phone to her mother, voice thick, saying she felt alone in a full hostel. I've left a note under her door with the counselling centre's evening hours, and I'll check in at breakfast.
Elizabeth

qa.q: How long did Disha's boyfriend wait at the gate?
qa.a: For an hour.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling as she held a book without turning a page?
qa.a: She seemed tense and lonely, avoiding a deep talk while feeling alone in a full hostel.

qa.q: How is Elizabeth supporting Disha?
qa.a: By leaving the counselling centre's hours under her door and planning a breakfast check-in, without pushing.

qa.q: What is it like for the boyfriend to wait an hour and get "busy"?
qa.a: He probably feels hurt and shut out, wanting to talk about the relationship and getting no answer.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who guards independence and avoids a deep conversation, while lonely inside.

passage:
Tuesday, 11.40 p.m. Parul asked tonight if we could spend Diwali with her family in Lucknow. I said I had a project, which is half true. Then she said, softly, "Sometimes it feels like you keep one foot out the door." I laughed it off and went home early. Now I'm lying here with the fan clicking, and I feel horrible, and also relieved, which is worse. I tell everyone I love my freedom. I do. But tonight the flat is so quiet I can hear the fridge. What scares me isn't Parul. It's how much I'd miss her if I let myself lean. Maybe I'll text her in the morning: "Sorry I left. Can we talk?"
Elizabeth

qa.q: Where does Parul's family live?
qa.a: In Lucknow.

qa.q: What mix of feelings does Elizabeth describe after leaving early?
qa.a: Elizabeth feels horrible and relieved at once, and scared of how much it would hurt to depend on Parul.

qa.q: What could Elizabeth try next?
qa.a: Send the planned message and share a little of the fear with Parul, instead of leaving again.

qa.q: How might Parul feel when Elizabeth laughs off her words?
qa.a: Parul probably feels hurt and brushed aside, having said something honest and vulnerable.

grounding: Shows a young adult who avoids deep talk and leaves when a partner asks for more, while fearing dependence and feeling lonely.
